operational_definition: Reported actions through which a message is selected, linguistically realised, delivered or presented, or communication trouble is addressed.
analytic_boundary: Action-level attribution framework; not a competence construct, fixed event sequence, or exhaustive taxonomy.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Study-specific operationalisation informed by communication-strategy, interactional, production-format and scaffolding research.

operational_definition: Specific episode; recurring-practice description; evaluative or hypothetical statement.
analytic_boundary: Only explicitly ordered accounts support timing; evaluations can explain participant reasoning but do not establish performed action or outcome.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Evidence-calibration rule for retrospective qualitative interviews.

operational_definition: Who determines what is to be requested, conveyed, or accomplished.
analytic_boundary: Selecting a meaning or goal does not establish who generated the Chinese wording.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Action dimension developed to separate communicative intention from linguistic realisation.

operational_definition: Who or what supplies the linguistic material used in the contribution.
analytic_boundary: External wording establishes provenance, not delegation; wording can be selected, adapted or delivered by the learner.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Related to production-role and distributed-action distinctions without equating them.

operational_definition: Who speaks, sends, shows or otherwise presents the contribution; mode is recorded separately.
analytic_boundary: Visual display, writing and speech are distinct modes; externally supplied wording can coexist with learner delivery.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Action dimension informed by production-format and participation research.

operational_definition: An explicitly reported action taken in response to difficulty understanding or being understood.
analytic_boundary: Retrospective functional category; not a reconstructed conversation-analytic repair sequence.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Bounded by interactional and communication-strategy research.

operational_definition: Reported progress, explicit practical completion, explicit failure, or unestablished outcome.
analytic_boundary: Outcome does not establish who carried message choice, wording, delivery or trouble management.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Complementary to functional-adequacy research; not an equivalent rating.

operational_definition: Whether the activity pathway required a specified communicative action, especially spoken negotiation.
analytic_boundary: Required, not required, and unestablished are kept separate from what was actually performed.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Activity-organisation boundary identified in the present corpus.

operational_definition: Whether the specified communicative action was reported as performed, explicitly not performed, or unestablished.
analytic_boundary: Occurrence is recorded separately from requirement so voluntary action remains visible even when an activity does not require it.

operational_definition: Learner; another person; tool; shared; unestablished, applied separately to each specified function.
analytic_boundary: Unestablished denotes insufficient evidence, not absence; applicability and activity requirement are separate.

operational_definition: Not applicable is a separate flag used only when the account explicitly establishes that the specified action did not occur, leaving no performance to attribute.
analytic_boundary: Not an actor category. Not required, nonmention, and qualified reports of little speech do not establish non-occurrence. Scope the decision to a specified action and account.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Clarification of the reporting rule; not evidence of additional recoding or a newly observed event.
illustrative_case_ids: Rule boundary; #60 must not be treated as universal absence of speech

operational_definition: More than one actor or resource contributes to the same specified communicative function.
analytic_boundary: Different actors performing different functions constitute mixed allocation, not automatically shared performance of each function.

operational_definition: Speech, writing, visual display, gesture, or multimodal presentation/management.
analytic_boundary: Mode does not establish wording authorship, message choice, or degree of participation.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Mode-sensitive descriptor used across supported encounters.

operational_definition: Reported choice, control, listening, gesture, presentation, mode selection or other action contributing to the activity.
analytic_boundary: Do not infer passivity from externally supplied wording or unestablished Chinese production.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Jointly organised participation; not limited to linguistic authorship.

operational_definition: An explicit handover or another person performing a specified communicative action on the learner's behalf.
analytic_boundary: Tool use or external wording alone is insufficient; delegation is action-specific rather than a whole-person label.

operational_definition: Different action dimensions have different attributed actors, resources or modes.
analytic_boundary: Known and unknown dimensions remain separate rather than being forced into learner-only/tool-only categories.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Interpretive refinement within the attribution procedure.

operational_definition: Use of persistent text for translation, copying, retyping, revision or delayed response.
analytic_boundary: Written control does not establish original Chinese composition or transfer to synchronous speech.

operational_definition: An interface completes practical steps while reducing or removing the need for a communicative action such as spoken negotiation.
analytic_boundary: Removal of a requirement is not delegated speech; other work can be relocated into reading, translation or interface management.
relationship_to_prior_literature: Boundary between activity organisation and action attribution.
